query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloys, the coexistence of chemically and electrochemically distinct phases (e.g., an FCC matrix with embedded σ or Laves phases) produces localized galvanic cells. At elevated temperature, the protective oxide films formed on these phases are repeatedly removed by wear, exposing fresh material and accelerating both wear and corrosion in a synergistic manner.
generation.material_initial_state: A multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a dual-phase microstructure comprised of an FCC matrix intermixed with harder second phases such as σ-phase precipitates.
generation.intervention: Conduct a controlled comparison by processing two alloys with identical overall compositions: one retaining the natural multiphase eutectic microstructure and the other processed (via post-solidification heat treatment or hot working) to achieve a homogeneous single-phase structure.
generation.conditions: Testing under simultaneous elevated temperature and wear-corrosive conditions (e.g., a pin-on-disk test at approximately 600°C in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under controlled load and sliding speed).
generation.structural_mediator: Interphase boundaries that serve as micro-galvanic couples due to differences in chemical potential between the phases; these boundaries facilitate localized anodic dissolution when the protective oxide film is mechanically removed by wear.
generation.mechanism: Localized galvanic corrosion at phase boundaries, where differences in electrochemical potential accelerate anodic dissolution. This is compounded by wear-induced rupture of protective oxide films at elevated temperatures, leading to a feedback loop that enhances both corrosion and wear degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a single-phase baseline alloy, the multiphase eutectic alloy will experience higher total degradation: increased wear rates (manifesting as greater material loss and more pronounced wear scars) and accelerated corrosion (evidenced by lower corrosion potentials and higher corrosion current densities).
generation.baseline: A homogeneous single-phase high-entropy alloy of the same bulk composition, expected to form a more uniform and stable passive oxide film with reduced galvanic coupling.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions where both high temperature (around 600°C) and simultaneous mechanical wear in a corrosive medium (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl) are present, ensuring that both wear and corrosion mechanisms can interact.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative mechanism is supported, the quantitative increase in degradation rates is uncertain and may depend strongly on the exact phase morphology, distribution, and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloys with identical overall compositions: one set with the natural multiphase eutectic microstructure and a second set treated (by homogenizing heat treatment) to achieve a single-phase structure. Subject both sets to identical pin-on-disk wear tests in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at 600°C. Record mass loss, wear scar morphology, friction coefficients, and electrochemical parameters (via potentiodynamic polarization and impedance spectroscopy) over the same test duration.
measurements: Total mass loss and wear scar dimensions
Corrosion potential and current density from electrochemical measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multiphase eutectic alloy does not demonstrate statistically significant higher degradation (in terms of both increased wear rates and accelerated corrosion parameters) compared to the homogenized single-phase alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. This study systematically investigates the microstructure evolution, tribological properties, and corrosion mechanisms of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings fabricated via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding under variable laser power conditions. The key findings and implications are summarized as follows: The CoCrFeNiMo coatings exhibited a dual-phase structure comprising FCC and σ phases. At 2250 W, optimized energy density promoted homogeneous dispersion of Fe-Cr-rich σa and Fe-Mo-rich σb phases within the FCC matrix, forming a refined eutectic–hypereutectic hybrid microstructure. The hardness of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coatings increased with laser power, peaking at 738.3 HV0.2 at 2250 W. This improvement was attributed to solution strengthening and second-phase intensification. However, at 2000 W, the hardness decreased due to grain coarsening caused by the extended molten pool duration. At a laser power of 2250 W, the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating exhibited the lowest coefficient of friction (COF = 0.084) and excellent wear resistance.
